Content:
A Treatise of Civil Power

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](./Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)

Notes
-----

1. [↑](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-1) Shawcross 1993 p. 172
2. [↑](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-2) Mueller 1998 pp. 21–38
3. [1](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-Milton_p._246_3-0) [2](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-Milton_p._246_3-1) Milton 1974 p. 246
4. [↑](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-4) Achinstein 2003 p. 421
5. [↑](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-5) Shawcross 1993 p. 129
6. [↑](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-6) Keeble 2003 p. 129
7. [↑](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-7) Rumrich 2003 p. 151
8. [↑](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-8) Shawcross 1993 p. 240
9. [↑](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-9) Corns 2003 p. 92
10. [↑](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_ref-10) Hart, Kevin (April 2008). ["Poetics and Power | Kevin Hart"](https://www.firstthings.com/article/2008/04/003-poetics-and-power). *First Things*. Retrieved 2021-01-28.

References
----------

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

A Treatise of Civil Power

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](./Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

A Treatise of Civil Power

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](./Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

A Treatise of Civil Power

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](./Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)

If an [internal link](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Special:Whatlinkshere/Andraemon&namespace=0) for a specific Greek mythology article referred you to this page, you may wish to change the link to point directly to the intended Greek mythology article, if one exists.\\nURL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power\\n\\nStatus Code: 200\\n\\nContent:\\nA Treatise of Civil Power\\n\\n***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist \"Polemicist\") [John Milton](./John_Milton \"John Milton\") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy \"Heresy\") and [free thought](./Free_thought \"Free thought\"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament \"English Parliament\") to further his cause.\\n\\nThe work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector \"Lord Protector\") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell \"Richard Cromwell\"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual\\'s conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion \"Freedom of religion\") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion \"State religion\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell \"Richard Cromwell\") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum \"Interregnum\") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\nAlthough Milton knew that the word \"heresy\" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as \"only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning\".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved \"by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit\".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)\\n\\nThe text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) \"Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis\\'d on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union\".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\nMilton believed that an individual\\'s conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains \"A fusion of submission and revolution\".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton\\'s earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) \"Kevin Hart (poet)\") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things \"First Things\")*, \"His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language.\"[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n1. Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

A Treatise of Civil Power

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](./Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

A Treatise of Civil Power

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](./Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

A Treatise of Civil Power

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](./Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

A Treatise of Civil Power

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](./Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

If an [internal link](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Special:Whatlinkshere/Andraemon&namespace=0) for a specific Greek mythology article referred you to this page, you may wish to change the link to point directly to the intended Greek mythology article, if one exists.\\nURL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power\\n\\nStatus Code: 200\\n\\nContent:\\nA Treatise of Civil Power\\n\\n***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist \"Polemicist\") [John Milton](./John_Milton \"John Milton\") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy \"Heresy\") and [free thought](./Free_thought \"Free thought\"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament \"English Parliament\") to further his cause.\\n\\nThe work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector \"Lord Protector\") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell \"Richard Cromwell\"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual\\'s conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion \"Freedom of religion\") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion \"State religion\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell \"Richard Cromwell\") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum \"Interregnum\") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\nAlthough Milton knew that the word \"heresy\" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as \"only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning\".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved \"by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit\".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)\\n\\nThe text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) \"Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis\\'d on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union\".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\nMilton believed that an individual\\'s conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains \"A fusion of submission and revolution\".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton\\'s earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) \"Kevin Hart (poet)\") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things \"First Things\")*, \"His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language.\"[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n1. 200\\n\\nContent:\\nAndraemon\\n\\nIn [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology \"Greek mythology\") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English \"Help:IPA/English\"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language \"Ancient Greek language\"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek \"Romanization of Ancient Greek\"):\\xa0*Andraímon*) may refer to:\\n\\n* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus \"Oxylus\") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) \"Dryope (daughter of Dryops)\").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)\\n* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)\\n* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia \"Aetolia\") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) \"Gorge (mythology)\") of [Calydon](./Calydon \"Calydon\"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) \"Thoas (king of Aetoila)\"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus \"Oeneus\")\\' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia \"Aetolia\"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa \"Amfissa\").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)\\n* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) \"Leonteus (mythology)\"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome \"Amphinome\"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias \"Pelias\").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)\\n* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope \"Suitors of Penelope\") of [Penelope](./Penelope \"Penelope\") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium \"Dulichium\") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus \"Odysseus\") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus \"Eumaeus\"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) \"Philoetius (Odyssey)\"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus \"Telemachus\").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)\\n* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus \"Codrus\"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor \"Asia Minor\") and drove the [Carians](./Caria \"Caria\") out of the city of Lebedus. If an [internal link](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Special:Whatlinkshere/Andraemon&namespace=0) for a specific Greek mythology article referred you to this page, you may wish to change the link to point directly to the intended Greek mythology article, if one exists.\\nURL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power\\n\\nStatus Code: 200\\n\\nContent:\\nA Treatise of Civil Power\\n\\n***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist \"Polemicist\") [John Milton](./John_Milton \"John Milton\") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy \"Heresy\") and [free thought](./Free_thought \"Free thought\"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament \"English Parliament\") to further his cause.\\n\\nThe work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector \"Lord Protector\") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell \"Richard Cromwell\"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual\\'s conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion \"Freedom of religion\") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion \"State religion\").\\n\\nBackground\\n----------\\n\\n*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell \"Richard Cromwell\") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum \"Interregnum\") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)\\n\\nTract\\n-----\\n\\nAlthough Milton knew that the word \"heresy\" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as \"only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning\".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved \"by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit\".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)\\n\\nThe text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) \"Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis\\'d on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union\".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)\\n\\nThemes\\n------\\n\\nMilton believed that an individual\\'s conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains \"A fusion of submission and revolution\".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton\\'s earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) \"Kevin Hart (poet)\") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things \"First Things\")*, \"His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language.\"[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)\\n\\nNotes\\n-----\\n\\n1. Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

A Treatise of Civil Power

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](./Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)

Andraemon

In [Greek mythology](./Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") the name **Andraemon** ([/ænˈdriːmən/](./Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Ancient Greek](./Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀνδραίμων, [romanized](./Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Andraímon*) may refer to:

* Andraemon, son of [Oxylus](./Oxylus "Oxylus") and husband of [Dryope](./Dryope_(daughter_of_Dryops) "Dryope (daughter of Dryops)").[[1]](./Andraemon#cite_note-1)
* Andraemon, possible father of another Oxylus.[[2]](./Andraemon#cite_note-2)
* Andraemon, an [Aetolian](./Aetolia "Aetolia") king and husband of [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)") of [Calydon](./Calydon "Calydon"). By the latter, he became the father of [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"). Andraemon succeeded his father-in-law [Oeneus](./Oeneus "Oeneus")' power over [Aetolia](./Aetolia "Aetolia"). He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](./Amfissa "Amfissa").[[3]](./Andraemon#cite_note-3)
* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](./Leonteus_(mythology) "Leonteus (mythology)"). He married [Amphinome](./Amphinome "Amphinome"), a daughter of [Pelias](./Pelias "Pelias").[[4]](./Andraemon#cite_note-4)
* Andraemon, one of the [Suitors](./Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") of [Penelope](./Penelope "Penelope") who came from [Dulichium](./Dulichium "Dulichium") along with other 56 wooers.[[5]](./Andraemon#cite_note-5) He, with the other suitors, was slain by [Odysseus](./Odysseus "Odysseus") with the aid of [Eumaeus](./Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), [Philoetius](./Philoetius_(Odyssey) "Philoetius (Odyssey)"), and [Telemachus](./Telemachus "Telemachus").[[6]](./Andraemon#cite_note-6)
* Andraemon, a son of King [Codrus](./Codrus "Codrus"). He participated in the colonization of [Asia Minor](./Asia_Minor "Asia Minor") and drove the [Carians](./Caria "Caria") out of the city of Lebedus. His tomb was shown near [Colophon](./Colophon_(city) "Colophon (city)").[[7]](./Andraemon#cite_note-7) [Mimnermus](./Mimnermus "Mimnermus") related that Andraemon was a native of [Pylos](./Pylos "Pylos") and founder of Colophon.[[8]](./Andraemon#cite_note-8)

Similarly **Andraemonides** was a [patronymic](./Patronymic "Patronymic"), frequently used to refer to [Thoas](./Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"), son of Andraemon and [Gorge](./Gorge_(mythology) "Gorge (mythology)").[[9]](./Andraemon#cite_note-9)

A Treatise of Civil Power

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](./Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](./John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](./Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](./Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](./English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](./Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](./Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](./State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](./Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](./Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](./Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](./First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](./A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power#cite_note-10)
